classification_signals: Abstract mentions 'Research on human spatial memory and navigational ability has recently shown...' and 'The navigability and usability of built space is systematically analysed in the light of cognitive theories...'
Section 2.2 'Alignment Effects in Spatial Memory' reviews empirical studies, including the authors' own work (e.g., Werner, Saade, & Lüer, 1998; Werner & Schmidt, 1999).

Section 4.3 'Misalignment of Local Reference Systems as a Wayfinding Problem: Two Examples' presents two case studies (Göttingen town hall, Downtown Minneapolis) and explicitly states: 'In a small experiment we tested these types of map arrangements against each other and found that observers had an easier time interpreting and using spatial information... (Werner & Jaeger, 2002).'
The paper integrates theoretical discussions with empirical findings (both cited and from the authors' own work) and qualitative observations (informal interviews in Example 1).
title: Cognition Meets Le Corbusier - Cognitive Principles of Architectural Design

findings.consequent: Accessing spatial information in navigation and other spatially oriented tasks
findings.quote: Research on human spatial memory and navigational ability has recently shown the strong influence of reference systems in spatial memory

findings.antecedent: Misalignment between the reference system used to encode spatial information in memory and the reference system required by a particular task
findings.quote: a large cognitive cost, both in terms of speed and accuracy that occurs whenever the reference system used to encode spatial information in memory is not aligned with the reference system required by a particular task.

findings.antecedent: Alignment of 'You-are-here' (YAH) map's up-down direction with observer's front-back direction
findings.consequent: Comprehension and use of map information
findings.quote: Observers more easily comprehend and use information depicted in "You-are-here” (YAH) maps if the up-down direction of the map coincides with the front-back direction of the observer.

findings.antecedent: Observer's viewpoint aligned with encoding viewpoint (when viewing a path with multiple segments)
findings.consequent: Retrieval ease of spatial relations from memory
findings.quote: human observers have an easier time retrieving from memory the spatial relations between locations as seen from this viewpoint than from other, misaligned views or headings

findings.antecedent: Imagined heading aligned with the first learned viewpoint (when learning object locations from multiple viewpoints)
findings.consequent: Speed and correctness of response in spatial memory tasks
findings.quote: he will be fastest and most correct in his response when imagining himself in the same heading as the first view.

findings.antecedent: Imagined alignment with a square room's two main axes (parallel to walls) vs. diagonals
findings.consequent: Retrieval ease of spatial knowledge about the configuration
findings.quote: she will have a much easier time retrieving the spatial knowledge about the configuration when imagining herself aligned with the room's two main axes parallel to the walls than when imagining herself aligned with the two diagonals of the room.

findings.antecedent: Imagined alignment with a city's street grid
findings.consequent: Ease of imagining oneself aligned for pointing tasks to landmarks
findings.quote: participants have a much easier time imagining themselves aligned with the street grid than misaligned with the street grid
the perceived structure of an environment influences the way a space is mentally represented

findings.antecedent: Imagined alignment with the steepest gradient (uphill/downhill) in a sloped environment
findings.consequent: Speed and accuracy of accessing spatial knowledge
findings.quote: Accessing spatial knowledge about this sloped environment was fastest and most accurate when imagining oneself facing uphill or downhill, thus aligning oneself with the steepest gradient of the space

findings.consequent: Ease of navigation within a building
findings.quote: the complexity of the floor plan has a significant influence on the ease with which users can navigate within a building

findings.antecedent: ICD (inter-connection density) measure of floor plan complexity
findings.consequent: Empirical ratings of floor plan complexity
findings.quote: The correlation of the ICD measure and empirical ratings of complexity for the plans used in his study were fairly high.

findings.antecedent: Decreased symmetry, changed orientation, or decreased regularity of floor plans (with identical ICD)
findings.quote: Their perceived complexity, however, rises from left to right, by making the figures less symmetric, changing the orientation, or making the figure less regular.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design of Göttingen town hall (conflicting spatial reference systems)
findings.consequent: Navigational difficulty and low architectural legibility
findings.quote: Informal interviews with people working in or visiting this building revealed that it is difficult to understand and navigate. The architectural legibility is very low.

findings.antecedent: Conflicting spatial reference systems in different parts of an environment
findings.consequent: Navigational difficulties and difficulty integrating spatial knowledge
findings.quote: This misalignment between the parts makes integration of spatial knowledge very difficult.

findings.antecedent: Map information aligned with visual vertical and horizontal axes
findings.consequent: Ease of interpreting and using spatial information from maps, and accuracy of spatial relation judgments from memory
findings.quote: observers had an easier time interpreting and using spatial information gathered from a map in which the depicted information was aligned with the visual vertical and horizontal, whereas a misalignment with these axes led to more errors in judgements about spatial relations made from memory (Werner & Jaeger, 2002).

findings.consequent: Ability to integrate spatial information across multiple places
findings.quote: misalignment of reference systems impairs the users ability to integrate spatial information across multiple places.

findings.antecedent: Consistent alignment of reference axes throughout a building
findings.consequent: Cognitive load and ease of keeping track of position
findings.quote: the consistent alignment of reference axes throughout the building, all other things being equal, will greatly reduce the cognitive load while keeping track of once position.

findings.antecedent: Visual access to distant landmarks or common links (e.g., courtyard, atrium) within a building
findings.consequent: Support for wayfinding tasks (by providing access to a global frame of reference)
findings.quote: Providing navigators access to a global frame of reference within a building will greatly support wayfinding tasks. This can be achieved by providing visual access to distant landmarks or a common link, such as a courtyard or atrium.

limitations: The Inter-Connection Density (ICD) measure of floor plan complexity does not always correlate with perceived complexity, as perceived complexity can rise with decreased symmetry, changed orientation, or reduced regularity even when ICD is identical (p. 7).
The findings from the Göttingen town hall are based on 'informal interviews' (p. 11), which suggests a qualitative and potentially non-generalizable data collection method.
The empirical finding regarding map arrangements is from a 'small experiment' (p. 13), implying potential limitations in scope or generalizability.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper investigates how cognitive principles, particularly the alignment of spatial reference systems, impact human wayfinding and spatial memory in architectural design. It synthesizes existing research and presents observational case studies (Göttingen town hall, Downtown Minneapolis) and findings from a small experiment by the authors. Key findings indicate that misalignment between spatial reference systems used for encoding and task execution leads to increased cognitive load and errors in spatial judgments. The paper concludes with design recommendations, such as ensuring consistent alignment of reference axes and providing visual access to global landmarks, to enhance architectural legibility and support navigation. Limitations include the qualitative nature of some observations and the limited scope of the described experiment.
